metadata.title: What drives and drains teachers in Taiwan? Exploring the motivational roots of job satisfaction through stress pathways

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 secondary analysis for lower secondary (junior high) teachers in Taiwan and applies the TALIS complex survey design framework. Analyses are conducted on each of 20 multiple-imputed teacher-level datasets, and then pooled using Rubin’s combination rules after applying the final teacher weights. For variance estimation under the complex design, the authors also incorporate the provided 80 replicate weights using balanced repeated replication (BRR) with Fay’s adjustment factor 0.5, implemented by re-estimating the model across replicate weight sets and combining estimates to obtain robust standard errors. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., a W_ variable), but it explicitly states that final teacher weights and the 80 replicate weights were used in AMOS/SEM.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Secondary analysis of TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data restricted to lower secondary (junior high school) teachers in Taiwan. The analytic sample comprises 3598 teachers; the study does not describe additional exclusions beyond the multiple-imputation procedure for missing responses across key motivation, stress, and job satisfaction constructs. Imputation was performed at the teacher level prior to applying survey weights.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 Lower secondary (junior high) teachers, Taiwan
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM fit (measurement/structural): CFA χ2(120, N=3598)=700.45, CFI=0.981, TLI=0.975, RMSEA=0.034, SRMR=0.017; Structural χ2(132, N=3598)=764.174, CFI=0.979, TLI=0.972, RMSEA=0.035, SRMR=0.018. Direct effects on job satisfaction: β=0.07 (personal utility; p<.001), β=0.16 (social utility; p<.001), β=0.13 (intrinsic career value; p<.001), β=-0.18 (workload; p<.001), β=-0.20 (student behavior stress; p<.001). Indirect effects: personal utility via student behavior stress β=-0.02 (p<.001); social utility via workload β=0.01 (p<.05) and via student behavior stress β=0.02 (p<.001); intrinsic career value via workload β=0.03 (p<.001) and via student behavior stress β=0.02 (p<.001). Total associations: personal utility β_total=0.05 (p<.001), social utility β_total=0.19 (p<.001), intrinsic career value β_total=0.18 (p<.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 lower secondary (junior high) teacher data from Taiwan, the study leveraged personal utility motivation, social utility motivation, intrinsic career value, and stressors (perceived workload and student behavior stress) to model job satisfaction, finding that all three motivation types were positively associated with job satisfaction while both workload and student behavior stress were negatively associated. It further found that stress partially mediated these relationships: personal utility motivation increased student behavior stress (reducing satisfaction), whereas social utility and intrinsic career value reduced both workload and student behavior stress (increasing satisfaction). This indicates that strengthening intrinsic and prosocial motivation while reducing workload and classroom misbehavior pressures may improve teacher job satisfaction and well-being, though the cross-sectional SEM design limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study conducts a secondary analysis of TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data for 3,598 lower secondary (junior high) teachers in Taiwan, using a complex survey design with final teacher weights and 80 replicate weights (BRR with Fay’s adjustment factor 0.5). Missing responses across key constructs were handled via multiple imputation using Markov chain Monte Carlo (20 imputed datasets), with pooled estimates using Rubin’s combination rules. The authors estimate a multiple-mediator SEM in AMOS (maximum likelihood) and report strong model fit (structural model: χ2(132)=764.174, CFI=0.979, TLI=0.972, RMSEA=0.035, SRMR=0.018). Job satisfaction (T3JSENV) is positively predicted by personal utility (β=0.07), social utility (β=0.16), and intrinsic career value (β=0.13), while workload (β=-0.18) and student behavior stress (β=-0.20) are negative predictors. Mediation is supported by significant indirect paths (e.g., personal utility via student behavior stress β=-0.02; social utility via workload β=0.01 and via student behavior stress β=0.02). Limitations include correlational inference due to cross-sectional self-report measures and the absence of ML-based predictive evaluation.
